subject: mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 10 periods = 500 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 8h 20min

periods.activity_title: Naming the Parts of an Algebraic Expression

textbook_items_in_class.description: Pens-and-pencils scenario introducing terms, variables, coefficients, and constant in the expression 4x + 5y + 3.
Rectangular garden fencing and seeding cost scenario producing the two-variable expression 200l + 160w + 50lw.
Wire bent into a rectangle; area expressed as the one-variable expression x(10-x) = 10x - x^2.
Find the degrees of four given polynomials.
Find the coefficients of x^2 and x^3 in a given degree-4 polynomial.

time_bands.activity: Open with three everyday scenarios written on the board: the cost of buying pens and pencils, the cost of fencing and seeding a garden, and the area of a rectangle made from a bent wire. Ask students to write, in their own words, what is changing and what is fixed in each situation. Collect two or three responses aloud to surface the intuition that some quantities are unknown.

Walk through Example 1 (p.16) and Example 2 (p.16-17) together, building the expressions 4x + 5y + 3 and 200l + 160w + 50lw on the board. As each expression is built, label each part: term, variable, coefficient, constant. Then work through Example 3 (p.17), where a one-variable expression emerges from the wire-rectangle scenario, and name its degree. Ask students to examine all three expressions and identify what they have in common and where they differ — the think-and-reflect prompt — before introducing the formal definition of a univariate polynomial and naming cubic, quadratic, linear, and constant polynomials by degree.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 2.1 Q1 (p.18) — finding the degree of four polynomials — and Q3 (p.18) — identifying the coefficients of specific powers in a degree-4 polynomial. Circulate, checking that students are reading the highest power correctly and not confusing the coefficient of a term with its degree.

Bring the class together for a quick discussion: ask two students to share their answer to Q1 and one to share Q3, then address any disagreements on the board. Close by asking students to state, in one sentence, what the degree of a polynomial tells you.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's algebraic vocabulary, so the emphasis is on building precise language from concrete scenarios before stating formal definitions — the inductive move from the three examples to the definition. Watch for students who confuse the degree of a polynomial with the number of terms, or who read the coefficient of a term as its power. Example 3 (p.17) can be assigned as independent reading for students who finish the exercises early.
homework: Exercise Set 2.1 Q2, p.18 — write polynomials of degrees 1, 2, and 3 in any variable.
Exercise Set 2.1 Q4–5, p.19 — identify the coefficient of z and the constant term in given cubic polynomials.

periods.activity_title: Defining Linear Polynomials and Solving Linear Equations

textbook_items_in_class.description: Perimeter of a square of side x as the linear polynomial 4x.
Chess club joining fee plus per-match charge modelled as the linear polynomial 200 + 50m.
Sum-of-two-numbers word problem solved via the linear equation 2x + 10 = 64; also introduces evaluating a linear expression as an input-output process.
Evaluate the linear polynomial 5x-3 at three given values of x (sub-parts i-iii).
Find present ages of Salil and his mother from a linear-equation age relationship.
Find the dimensions of a rectangle given its perimeter and a relation between length and width.

time_bands.activity: Write two expressions on the board: 4x and 200 + 50m. Ask students to name the degree of each and identify the coefficient of the variable term and the constant. This surfaces the definition of a linear polynomial (degree 1, form ax + b) before the textbook states it. Briefly note the contrast with the quadratic x(10 - x) from Section 2.1.

Walk through Example 4 (p.19), Example 5 (p.19), and Example 6 (p.20) in sequence. For Example 5, pause at the think-and-reflect moment: ask students to compute the payment for 3 matches and then work backward — if the payment was ₹450, how many matches were played? This forward-and-backward exercise motivates the idea of a linear equation. In Example 6, make explicit the input-output view: the polynomial takes an input x and returns an output, and a linear equation fixes the output and asks for the input.

Students work on Exercise Set 2.2 Q1 (p.21) — evaluating 5x − 3 at three values — and two word problems: Q3 (p.21) on Salil and his mother's ages, and Q7 (p.21) on rectangle dimensions. For each word problem, require students to write the linear expression before solving the equation, not to guess and check.

Select one student's solution to Q3 and one to Q7 to share with the class. Highlight the structure: verbal scenario → linear expression → equation → solution. Address any case where a student set up the equation incorrectly before solving.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the vocabulary of polynomial terms and degrees in Section 2.1, this unit adds the defining characteristic of a linear polynomial — degree exactly 1 — and introduces the equation-solving move. The most common error at this stage is forming the equation incorrectly from the word problem, often by adding rather than equating; watch for students who write '2x + 10 + 64' instead of '2x + 10 = 64'. Exercise Set 2.2 Q2 (p.21), which evaluates a quadratic, can be assigned for self-study to reinforce the contrast between linear and quadratic evaluation.
homework: Exercise Set 2.2 Q4, p.21 — find two positive integers given their difference and ratio.
Exercise Set 2.2 Q5–6, p.21 — coin and fence-piece problems using linear equations.

periods.activity_title: From Growing Patterns to Linear Expressions
materials: Graph paper or squared paper (optional, for drawing tile patterns)

textbook_items_in_class.description: Bela's pocket money depletion modelled as 100 - 5n, solved for the day the amount left equals 40.
Auto-rickshaw fare with flat initial charge plus per-km rate, modelled as 15n - 5 for n >= 2.
Find a linear expression for a savings account balance growing by a fixed monthly amount.
Find a linear expression for rally membership decreasing by a fixed amount each hour.
Express remaining pages of a book read at a constant daily rate as a linear pattern.

time_bands.activity: Draw the square-tile pattern from the chapter on the board: stage 1 has 1 tile, stage 2 has 3 tiles, stage 3 has 5 tiles. Ask students to extend the pattern to stage 4 and stage 5, then list the sequence of tile counts. Prompt them to compute the difference between consecutive terms, then ask: can you write a formula that gives the number of tiles at stage n? Allow students to work in pairs and share their guesses. Lead the class to the expression 2n − 1, verifying it against stages 1–5, and formally define a linear pattern as a sequence with constant difference between consecutive terms.

Work through Example 7 (p.22-23) — Bela's pocket money — and Example 8 (p.23) — the auto-rickshaw fare. For each, use the think-and-reflect approach: first ask students to predict the value of the expression at a large stage (e.g., day 12 for Bela), then ask them to work backward from a given output to find the input — 'on which day does Bela have exactly ₹40?' Show how this backward step is a linear equation.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 2.3 Q1 (p.23), Q2 (p.24), and Q5 (p.24). Each question requires first identifying the constant difference, then writing the linear expression for the nth term, then evaluating or solving as directed. Circulate and check that students are finding the constant difference before writing the expression.

Class discussion: ask one student to share the expression they built for Q1 and another for Q2. Draw out the parallel structure: starting value plus (constant rate × n). Invite students to say, in their own words, what makes a sequence 'linear'.

periods.teacher_notes: Having modelled single-variable linear expressions and equations in Section 2.2, this unit asks students to discover the same structure inside a growing geometric and numeric pattern — a more inductive route to the same object. A common error is writing the constant difference as the expression itself (writing '2' instead of '2n − 1'), especially when the starting value is 0; prompt students to verify their expression at n = 1 before proceeding. Exercise Set 2.3 Q3 and Q4 (p.24), on rectangle area and box volume as linear patterns, are suitable for self-study by students who finish early.
homework: Exercise Set 2.3 Q3, p.24 — find rectangle areas for given breadths and the linear pattern representing area at fixed length.
End of Chapter Q5, p.37 — express savings growing at a fixed monthly rate as a linear pattern and evaluate after 6 months and 2 years.

periods.activity_title: Modelling Linear Growth and Linear Decay

textbook_items_in_class.description: Journey cost function C(d) = 100 + 60d illustrating linear growth via a table of values.
Water height in a tank h(t) = 3 - 0.5t illustrating linear decay via a table of values.
Model plant height growing at a constant monthly rate; find height after 7 months, tabulate, and justify linear growth (sub-parts i-iii).
Model a depreciating mobile phone value; find value after 3 years, tabulate, and justify linear decay (sub-parts i-iii).
Model a depleting prepaid telecom balance; write the equation, find when balance runs out, and tabulate (sub-parts i-iii).

time_bands.activity: Write two partial tables on the board side by side: one where a quantity increases by a fixed amount each step, one where it decreases. Ask students to label which is 'growth' and which is 'decay' and to write the linear expression for the nth row of each table. Collect answers to establish that growth has a positive rate and decay has a negative rate before opening the textbook.

Work through Example 9 (p.24) on journey cost C(d) = 100 + 60d and Example 10 (p.24-25) on water height h(t) = 3 − 0.5t. For each, build the table of values, identify the constant increase or decrease, and name the scenario as linear growth or decay. Use the think-and-reflect prompt for each: after building the table, ask students to evaluate the function at a new input value not in the table, then to reverse — given an output, find the input.

Students work on Exercise Set 2.4 Q1 (p.25), Q2 (p.25), and Q4 (p.26) in pairs. Each problem has three sub-parts: writing the expression, evaluating it, and constructing a table. Require them to label each scenario explicitly as linear growth or linear decay with a one-sentence justification based on the sign of the rate.

Brief whole-class check: ask one pair to share the expression and label for Q1 and another for Q2. Ensure the class can articulate the distinction — a constant positive increment is growth, a constant negative increment is decay — before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored linear patterns in sequences in Section 2.3, this unit applies the same structure to continuous real-world functions, introducing the function-notation view C(d) and h(t). A frequent error is treating a decay scenario as growth because the coefficient appears without its sign in the word problem — watch for students who write 0.5t instead of −0.5t in the water-height function. Exercise Set 2.4 Q3 (p.25-26) on village population growth is well-suited for self-study.
homework: Exercise Set 2.4 Q3, p.25-26 — model a growing village population, find population after 6 years, tabulate, and justify linear growth.

periods.activity_title: Finding a and b in y = ax + b from Two Data Points

textbook_items_in_class.description: Telecom data-billing scenario; finds a and b in y = ax + b from two given (x, y) pairs by solving simultaneous equations.
Find a and b in a learning-platform billing relation y = ax+b from two given module-count/bill pairs.
Find a and b in a gym court-rental billing relation y = ax+b from two given hour/bill pairs.
Find a and b in the Celsius-Fahrenheit linear relation from the freezing and boiling reference points.

time_bands.activity: Present a simple table on the board: a telecom service charges ₹150 for 2 GB and ₹250 for 4 GB. Ask students whether this could be a linear relationship, and if so, what additional information they would need to write y = ax + b for this situation. Collect suggestions — students will likely say they need two equations — before presenting the formal method.

Work through Example 11 (p.25-26) in full. Write the two simultaneous equations that arise from substituting each data point into y = ax + b, solve by subtracting one from the other to find a, then back-substitute to find b. After obtaining the values, carry out the think-and-reflect discussion: ask students to interpret a and b in real-world terms — what does the slope a represent in the billing context, and what does b represent? Record the interpretations on the board.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 2.5 Q1 (p.27), Q2 (p.27), and Q3 (p.27). All three follow the same method: substitute two data points, subtract to eliminate b, find a, back-substitute. Q3 (Celsius-Fahrenheit) is the richest context — encourage students to interpret a and b after solving.

Quick consolidation: ask one student to state the method in two steps (substitute both points → subtract to find a → back-substitute to find b) and another to give the real-world meaning of a in Q2. Correct any sign errors from the board-sharing before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the form y = ax + b through growth and decay scenarios in Section 2.4, this unit asks students to recover a and b from data — reversing the direction of reasoning. The most common error is subtracting the two equations in the wrong order and obtaining a negative a when it should be positive, or losing the sign of b during back-substitution; draw attention to this step explicitly. Exercise Set 2.5 Q3 on Celsius-Fahrenheit is a rich self-study item students can verify by checking their a and b against the known conversion formula.

periods.activity_title: Plotting Points and Drawing the Graph of a Linear Equation
periods.visual_aids: Coordinate axes drawn on the board with a plotted line for reference during discussion.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Plots five points and identifies the line y = 3x by observing the constant ratio between coordinates.
Plots five points and identifies the line through them (negative slope case).

time_bands.activity: Distribute graph paper. Ask students to plot the five points (0,0), (1,3), (2,6), (−1,−3), (−2,−6) on their own axes without telling them the relationship. Ask: what do you notice about these points? Can you draw a single straight line through all of them? What is the ratio y/x for each point?

Work through Example 12 (p.28-29): show how plotting two points is sufficient to draw a line, and how the ratio observation leads to y = 3x. Then work through Example 13 (p.29) for the negative-slope case, having students plot the points themselves before drawing the line. Use the think-and-reflect prompt from Section 2.6: ask students to name one more point that must lie on each line, and to explain how they know without plotting it.

Students work in pairs: each pair chooses any two points satisfying y = 2x − 1, plots them on graph paper, draws the line, and then checks a third point. They then repeat for y = −x + 3. The goal is to consolidate the two-point plotting method before the next unit's comparison of families of lines.

Whole-class share: collect one pair's graph for y = 2x − 1 on the board. Discuss: where does this line cross the y-axis? What is the steepness? Plant these as open questions — what determines where the line crosses the y-axis, and what determines its steepness — to be answered in the subsequent unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Section 2.6's algebraic work on slope and intercept rests on the mechanical skill of plotting two points and drawing a line; this unit secures that skill through direct practice before formal concepts are named. Students frequently reverse the x and y coordinates when plotting, writing (y, x) instead of (x, y) — enforce the convention explicitly when students plot their first point. Example 13 (p.29) on the negative-slope case is worth assigning as self-study before students attempt families of lines.

periods.activity_title: Slope, Intercept, and Families of Lines on Shared Axes
periods.visual_aids: Board graphs comparing y = (1/2)x, y = x, y = 2x and y = 2x-1, y = 2x+1, y = 2x+5 to illustrate slope and intercept effects.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Graphs y = (1/2)x, y = x, y = 2x together to compare slope steepness as a varies for a > 0.
Graphs y = -(1/3)x, y = -x, y = -3x together to compare slope steepness as a varies for negative slopes.
Graphs y = 2x-1, y = 2x+1, y = 2x+5 individually and together, and y = x+3, y = 2x+5, y = 3x-2 together, to establish slope and y-intercept and the parallel-lines property.
Draw five sets of lines (sub-parts i-v) and reflect on the role of slope a and y-intercept b in each set.

time_bands.activity: Draw y = (1/2)x, y = x, and y = 2x on shared axes on the board (Example 14, p.29-31), plotting two points for each. Ask students: all three pass through the origin — what differs? Guide the class to name the steepness difference and to state formally that a is the slope, with larger |a| producing a steeper line. Then draw the three negative-slope lines from Example 15 (p.31-33) and ask students to compare them: what happens as |a| grows when a is negative?

Work through Example 16 (p.33-36): first the family y = 2x − 1, y = 2x + 1, y = 2x + 5 on shared axes. Ask students to state where each line crosses the y-axis, then to observe that all three are parallel. Introduce b as the y-intercept formally. Then draw y = x + 3, y = 2x + 5, y = 3x − 2 together and ask students to use the think-and-reflect prompt: compare the graphs as both a and b vary, and articulate a rule connecting the sign of a to the direction (growth or decay) of the graph.

Students work on at least three sub-parts of Exercise Set 2.6 Q1 (p.36) on their graph paper, drawing the specified families and writing one sentence per family describing the role of a or b. Circulate and confirm that students are reading the y-intercept correctly and naming parallel lines accurately.

Consolidation: ask two students to share their graphs and sentences for two different sub-parts. Close by having the class state, in unison, two things they can read off a linear equation y = ax + b before drawing it: the slope and the y-intercept.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the plotting skill established in the preceding unit on Section 2.6, this unit moves to the deductive claim: a governs steepness and sign, b governs the y-intercept, and equal a values produce parallel lines. A common confusion is between 'steeper' and 'larger b' — students sometimes say the line with b = 5 is 'higher' and conflate this with steepness; use the shared-axes drawings to separate the two properties sharply. Exercise Set 2.6 Q1 sub-parts iv and v are particularly rich for consolidating the parallel-lines property and are worth assigning as self-study.
homework: Exercise Set 2.6 Q1 sub-parts iv and v (p.36) — draw and compare two further families of lines and write one sentence each on the role of a and b.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Section 2.1–2.3: Polynomials, Equations, and Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write a degree-3 polynomial in x with a specified coefficient of the x^2 term.
Evaluate two given polynomials at specified values of the variable (sub-parts i-ii).
Find a number from a linear equation describing multiplying and adding fractions.
Find two numbers given one is 5 times the other and a relation after adding 21 to both.
Express savings growing at a fixed monthly rate as a linear pattern and evaluate after 6 months and 2 years.

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: write three polynomials on the board and ask students to state, without calculation, the degree and the coefficient of the highest-power term of each. Collect answers orally to reset the vocabulary from Section 2.1 before moving to the end-of-chapter questions.

Students work individually on End of Chapter Q1 (p.36) — constructing a degree-3 polynomial with a specified coefficient — and Q2 (p.36) — evaluating two polynomials at given values. Circulate, ensuring that students who evaluate the quadratic in Q2 (ii) are substituting t = a algebraically, not numerically.

Students tackle End of Chapter Q3 (p.37) and Q4 (p.37), both of which require building a linear equation from a verbal description and solving it. For Q3 the fractions add arithmetic complexity; for Q4 the two-quantity structure mirrors Exercise Set 2.2 word problems. Require students to write the linear expression before setting up the equation. Close this section with Q5 (p.37): express the savings pattern as a linear expression and evaluate at n = 6 and n = 24.

Class review: pick the two most commonly mis-set-up equations from Q3 and Q4 and work through them on the board, showing the translation from words to expression to equation. For Q5, confirm that students identified the constant difference correctly and that their expression passes the n = 1 check.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the vocabulary work of Section 2.1, the equation-solving of Section 2.2, and the pattern-expression work of Section 2.3 through end-of-chapter items. The fractional linear equation in Q3 is the most algebraically demanding item — watch for errors when multiplying both sides to clear denominators. Q2 (ii), which evaluates a cubic at t = a, is a self-study item with a non-numerical answer that stronger students can explore independently.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Sections 2.4–2.5: Growth, Decay, and Two-Variable Relationships

textbook_items_in_class.description: Model a growing village population; find population after 6 years, tabulate, and justify linear growth (sub-parts i-iii).
Model a depleting prepaid telecom balance; write the equation, find when balance runs out, and tabulate (sub-parts i-iii).
Find a and b in a learning-platform billing relation y = ax+b from two given module-count/bill pairs.
Find a and b in a gym court-rental billing relation y = ax+b from two given hour/bill pairs.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'A prepaid balance starts at ₹500 and decreases by ₹30 per call. After how many calls is the balance zero?' Ask students to write the expression, classify it as growth or decay, and solve the equation. This focuses the vocabulary from Section 2.4 before addressing the exercise items.

Students work on Exercise Set 2.4 Q3 (p.25-26) on village population and Q4 (p.26) on the prepaid telecom balance. For each, all three sub-parts must be completed: expression, evaluation, and table. In Q4, the 'when does balance run out?' sub-part is a linear equation — connect this back to the equation-solving structure from Section 2.2. Circulate and check that decay expressions carry a negative coefficient.

Students move on to Exercise Set 2.5 Q1 (p.27) and Q2 (p.27), finding a and b from two data points. These were introduced in Section 2.5; this session gives additional practice. For each, students must substitute both data points, subtract the equations, solve for a, and back-substitute for b. Ask students to write one sentence interpreting a and b in the real-world context of each problem.

Brief whole-class check on Q1 and Q2 from Exercise Set 2.5. Write one student's solution on the board, check the arithmetic, then ask the class: what would happen to the graph of this relationship if a were larger? Foreshadow the graphical interpretation without resolving it here.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the modelling work from Sections 2.4 and 2.5, bringing together growth and decay expression-building with the two-data-point method for finding a and b. Watch for students who, in the Q3 and Q4 tables, compute non-integer values and become uncertain — reassure them that a linear expression need not produce whole-number outputs at every step. In Q4 of Exercise Set 2.4, the moment when the balance reaches zero corresponds to an equation that may yield a non-integer answer, which is worth discussing.

periods.activity_title: Bringing Together the Chapter: Modelling, Graphing, and Interpreting
periods.visual_aids: Board graph showing a line y = ax + b with slope and y-intercept labelled, used to anchor the final discussion.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find a and b in the Celsius-Fahrenheit linear relation from the freezing and boiling reference points.
Draw five sets of lines (sub-parts i-v) and reflect on the role of slope a and y-intercept b in each set.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Exercise Set 2.5 Q3 (p.27) — the Celsius-Fahrenheit conversion — deriving a and b from the freezing and boiling data points. After solving, ask students to write, in one sentence, what a (the slope) and b (the intercept) mean in this context: a is the rate of change of Fahrenheit per degree Celsius, and b is the Fahrenheit value when Celsius is zero.

Draw the line y = (9/5)x + 32 on the board using graph paper axes (or the graph paper students now have). Mark the y-intercept at (0, 32) and compute one more point to draw the line. Then connect the graphical picture to the algebraic result: the slope is a = 9/5 and is positive, confirming linear growth; the y-intercept is b = 32. Ask students: is this a growth or a decay relationship? How do you know from the sign of a?

Students complete any remaining sub-parts of Exercise Set 2.6 Q1 (p.36) not yet done, focusing on the sub-parts that vary b with a fixed and then vary a with b fixed. For each family they draw, they write the two-sentence reflection on the role of a and b. These graphs bring together the graphical language of Section 2.6 with the algebraic content of Section 2.5.

Closing synthesis: draw on the board the schematic — real-world scenario → y = ax + b → graph. Ask three students to name one chapter scenario each and state which element of the schematic it illustrates: building the expression, solving for a and b, or reading the graph. Confirm that slope and y-intercept have both algebraic and graphical meaning, and that the sign of a determines growth or decay.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings the chapter's modelling spine — verbal scenario to y = ax + b to graph — into explicit view by completing the Celsius-Fahrenheit derivation and then graphing the resulting line. Watch for students who confuse the y-intercept of the Celsius-Fahrenheit line (32) with the slope, since 32 is the more memorable number; the intercept is where x = 0, not the rate of change. Exercise Set 2.5 Q1 and Q2 make good parallel self-study items for students who want additional practice with the two-data-point method.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the degree and the coefficient of a specified term in a given polynomial.

competency.competency_text: Model real-world situations as linear expressions and equations and solve them.

questions.question_text: Consider the polynomial p(x) = 5x^4 - 3x^3 + 7x^2 - x + 9. What is the coefficient of x^3 in this polynomial?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student reads the coefficient of x^3 as positive 3, ignoring the negative sign written in front of the term — a sign-reading error on the coefficient.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reports the power of the term (x^3 has power 3, so exponent is 3 but degree of the term containing x^3 is 3 not 4) — confusing the exponent with the coefficient, but picking 4 as the degree of the polynomial rather than the coefficient of x^3.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student reads the coefficient of the adjacent term x^2 (which is 7) instead of the coefficient of x^3 — confusion between adjacent terms.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who struggle, invite them to underline the x^3 term and write out just that term in isolation before identifying the number in front of it. For students ready for a challenge, ask them to write a different degree-4 polynomial where the coefficient of x^3 is the same as its degree.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a polynomial as constant, linear, quadratic, or cubic based on its degree.
questions.section_context: terms, variables, coefficients, degree, naming polynomials by degree

competency.competency_text: Model real-world situations as linear expressions and equations and solve them.

questions.question_text: Which of the following polynomials is correctly classified as quadratic?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student classifies a cubic polynomial (degree 3) as quadratic — confusing quadratic with any polynomial that contains an x^2 term, even if a higher-power term is present.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student classifies a linear polynomial (degree 1) as quadratic — likely recalling that 'quadratic' sounds like a two-term polynomial rather than a degree-2 polynomial.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student classifies a constant polynomial (degree 0) as quadratic — may have no clear understanding of degree and is guessing.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who need support, ask them to write the degree of each option beside it before choosing. For students ready for extension, ask them to construct one example of each polynomial type (constant, linear, quadratic, cubic) in a single variable.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a linear polynomial at a given value and solve a linear equation formed by equating a linear polynomial to a constant.
questions.section_context: linear polynomial evaluation, linear equation formation and solution, word problems

competency.competency_text: Model real-world situations as linear expressions and equations and solve them.

questions.question_text: A linear polynomial is given as p(t) = 8t - 6. (i) Evaluate p(t) when t = 4. (ii) Find the value of t for which p(t) = 50.
questions.method_one_line: Substitute t = 4 directly into 8t - 6 for part (i); set 8t - 6 = 50 and solve for t by adding 6 to both sides then dividing by 8 for part (ii).

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle, suggest they write the polynomial with the value substituted in brackets — 8(4) - 6 — before computing. For a challenge, ask them to find a second value of t for which p(t) is a perfect square.

questions.question_text: A school library charges an annual membership fee of ₹120 plus ₹15 for every book borrowed during the year. Priya paid a total of ₹330 for the year. Write a linear equation for this situation and find the number of books Priya borrowed.
questions.expected_answer: Linear equation: 120 + 15n = 330. Number of books borrowed: n = 14.
questions.method_one_line: Set up 120 + 15n = 330, subtract 120 from both sides to get 15n = 210, then divide by 15.

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle, suggest they first write the expression for the total cost as a polynomial in n before equating it to 330. For a challenge, ask them to find what the total cost would be if Priya had borrowed twice as many books.

questions.question_text: A community library opens with 240 books. Every week, 18 new books are added to the collection. (a) Show that the number of books after n weeks forms a linear pattern by identifying the constant difference. (b) Write a linear expression for the number of books after n weeks. (c) Find the number of books after 11 weeks. (d) In which week will the collection first exceed 500 books? Justify your answer by solving a linear equation.
look_for: Correctly identifies the constant difference as 18 and names it as the reason the pattern is linear.
Writes the expression 240 + 18n (or equivalent) with correct coefficients.
Sets up and solves 240 + 18n > 500, obtaining n > 14.44…, and correctly concludes that the collection first exceeds 500 books after week 15.
Justifies the week-15 answer by checking both n = 14 (which gives 492, not exceeding 500) and n = 15 (which gives 510, exceeding 500).

ECR.inclusivity: For students who need support, suggest they first write the number of books at weeks 0, 1, 2, and 3 in a table and circle the differences before writing the expression. For students who finish quickly, ask them to find the week in which the collection would exceed 700 books and explain whether the same method applies.
ECR.lift_note: This item is the reasoning floor lift (Rule 6): the section's implied_lo sits at Application (write and evaluate/solve a linear pattern), and this item lifts it to Analysis by requiring the student to justify the pattern's linearity by identifying the constant difference and to reason about when an inequality is first satisfied, verifying the boundary case.

questions.question_text: A mobile phone was bought for ₹18,000. Its value decreases by ₹2,400 every year. Which expression correctly models the phone's value V (in ₹) after t years, and how is this scenario classified?

options.label: A
options.text: V(t) = 18000 - 2400t; linear decay because the value decreases by a constant amount each year.

options.label: B
options.text: V(t) = 18000 - 2400t; linear growth because the starting value 18000 is large.

options.label: C
options.text: V(t) = 18000 + 2400t; linear growth because 2400 is added each year.

options.label: D
options.text: V(t) = 2400t - 18000; linear growth because the coefficient of t is positive.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student adds 2400t instead of subtracting it, treating a decrease as an increase — the most common sign error when building a decay expression from a word description.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student subtracts the starting value from the rate term, reversing the role of the constant and the rate — a structural confusion about which quantity is fixed and which varies.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly writes the expression V(t) = 18000 - 2400t but classifies it as linear growth because the initial value 18000 is large — confusing the magnitude of the starting value with the direction of change.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who need support, suggest they compute V at t = 0 and t = 1 and check whether the result went up or down before choosing a label. For a challenge, ask them to find the year in which the phone's value first falls below ₹6,000.

questions.question_text: A water tank holds 120 litres when full. Water is drained at a constant rate of 8 litres per minute. (i) Write the function W(t) for the volume of water (in litres) remaining after t minutes. (ii) Find W(9). (iii) After how many minutes will the tank contain exactly 56 litres?
questions.expected_answer: (i) W(t) = 120 - 8t. (ii) W(9) = 120 - 72 = 48 litres. (iii) 120 - 8t = 56 gives 8t = 64, so t = 8 minutes.
questions.method_one_line: Write W(t) = 120 - 8t from the starting volume and drain rate; substitute t = 9 directly for part (ii); set 120 - 8t = 56 and solve for t for part (iii).

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle, suggest they build a small table — t = 0, 1, 2 — to confirm the expression matches the word description before using it. For a challenge, ask them to find the time at which the tank is exactly half full.

questions.question_text: A gym charges members for court rental according to the linear relationship y = ax + b, where x is the number of hours and y is the total charge in rupees. The data in the table shows two observed charges. Refer to the table provided. Find the values of a and b, and write the complete linear relationship.
questions.expected_answer: a = 90, b = 130. The relationship is y = 90x + 130.
questions.method_one_line: Substitute both data points into y = ax + b to form two equations, subtract the first from the second to find a = (580 - 310)/(5 - 2) = 90, then back-substitute into either equation to find b = 310 - 90(2) = 130.

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle, suggest they label the two equations as Equation 1 and Equation 2 explicitly and show the subtraction step clearly before dividing. For a challenge, ask them to interpret a = 90 and b = 130 in the context of the gym's billing structure and use the relationship to find the charge for 8 hours.

competency.competency_text: Use coordinate geometry to graph a linear equation and interpret its solution set.

questions.question_text: Plot the graph of y = 3x - 2 on the coordinate plane provided. Show the two points you use to draw the line and label them with their coordinates.
questions.expected_answer: Two valid points: (0, -2) and (2, 4) [or any two correct pairs satisfying y = 3x - 2, e.g. (1, 1)]. The line passes through these points and extends in both directions.
questions.method_one_line: Substitute two chosen x-values into y = 3x - 2 to obtain two (x, y) pairs, plot both on the coordinate plane, and draw a straight line through them.

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle, suggest they start with x = 0 to find the y-intercept easily, then try x = 1 or x = 2. For a challenge, ask them to identify the x-intercept (where the line crosses the x-axis) from the graph and verify it by solving 3x - 2 = 0.

questions.question_text: Three linear equations are given: (i) y = 4x + 1, (ii) y = 4x - 3, (iii) y = -2x + 1. Without drawing a graph, answer the following: (a) Which two lines are parallel? Give one reason using the values of a and b. (b) Which line has a negative slope, and what does this tell you about the direction of the graph?
expected_elements: Lines (i) y = 4x + 1 and (ii) y = 4x - 3 are parallel because they have the same slope a = 4.
The fact that b differs (1 vs -3) means they cross the y-axis at different points but never intersect.
Line (iii) y = -2x + 1 has a negative slope (a = -2), meaning the graph falls from left to right — it represents a decay relationship.

SCR.inclusivity: For students who need support, suggest they write out the value of a for each equation in a list and compare before answering. For a challenge, ask them to write a fourth equation that is parallel to line (iii) and crosses the y-axis above line (iii).
